title: ‘All Izz Well’ Again? Aamir Khan Confirms 3 Idiots Sequel With Original Cast — and Every NRI Just Felt 19 Again
excerpt: Rajkumar Hirani returns to direct. R. Madhavan and Sharman Joshi are expected back. The story picks up years later — and the diaspora that grew up quoting Rancho is losing its mind.
body:
There is a short list of Hindi films that every NRI has watched regardless of whether they actually like Hindi cinema. 3 Idiots sits at the top of that list, somewhere between a movie and a generational inside joke. If you went to university anywhere in the diaspora between 2010 and 2020, someone in your friend group quoted Rancho at least once a semester. Probably more.

Now Aamir Khan has confirmed what the rumour mills have chewed on for years: a sequel is in active development. Rajkumar Hirani is expected to direct. R. Madhavan and Sharman Joshi are set to return. The film will feature a significant time jump — though whether the story leaps forward or backward from the original’s timeline is being kept deliberately vague. According to industry sources, only Aamir Khan currently knows the full direction of the narrative.

What We Know So Far

The project is in pre-production. An official announcement with a confirmed cast list, production timeline, and release window is still pending. But the key ingredients — Aamir, Madhavan, Sharman, and Hirani — are all reportedly locked in, and Aamir has begun active work on the project.

The original 3 Idiots released in 2009, adapted loosely from Chetan Bhagat’s novel Five Point Someone. It followed three engineering students navigating India’s pressure-cooker education system while trying not to lose themselves in the process. The film grossed over ₹400 crore worldwide and became a cultural landmark — not just in India, but across East and Southeast Asia. In China, it remains one of the most-watched Indian films of all time.

The time-jump detail is intriguing. The original ended with a satisfying resolution: Rancho living as a scientist-teacher in Ladakh, Raju working at a corporation, Farhan pursuing wildlife photography. A sequel set years later raises obvious questions. Are the characters still where we left them? Has the Indian education system changed enough to give Hirani fresh material? And crucially — can a sequel capture the same emotional frequency that made the original feel like a warm hug from an old friend?

Why NRIs Care More Than Anyone

Here’s the thing about 3 Idiots in the diaspora: it wasn’t just a film. It was therapy. Every Indian kid who’d been pushed into engineering or medicine by well-meaning parents saw themselves in that story. Every NRI who’d moved abroad and wondered whether the degree was worth the pressure felt Rancho’s speech in their bones. “Chase excellence, success will follow” became the counter-argument at a thousand dinner tables.

The film crossed cultural barriers in ways few Hindi films have managed. Screenings at American universities. Watch parties in London flats. Pirated DVDs making the rounds in Gulf countries. 3 Idiots was the great equaliser — the one film every desi could agree on, regardless of language, region, or how long they’d been away from India.

A sequel arriving now, potentially 17 years after the original, lands at an interesting moment. The NRI kids who watched 3 Idiots in college are now in their thirties and forties — many of them parents themselves. The pressure-cooker education culture the film critiqued has only intensified, with Indian coaching centres now running satellite operations in the US and UK. The conversation Hirani started hasn’t ended; it’s just moved continents.

The Madhavan and Sharman Factor

Both actors have had fascinating trajectories since 2009. Madhavan reinvented himself as a filmmaker with Rocketry: The Nambi Effect (2022), playing ISRO scientist Nambi Narayanan — a role that earned widespread praise. Sharman Joshi has remained active in Hindi cinema and theatre, though without a breakout role matching the original. Their return promises nostalgia, but the real test will be whether Hirani can write them as grown men rather than echoes of their younger selves.

What Comes Next

No release date has been announced. Given Hirani’s meticulous production style — he typically takes 3-4 years between films — a 2028 or 2029 release seems realistic. But the mere confirmation is enough to set off the diaspora hype machine. Expect “All Izz Well” to trend globally within hours of an official announcement.

For NRIs who grew up on this film, one question remains: will the sequel make them feel 19 again — or remind them how much has changed since?
